text: Trucks are used to move jet fuel from terminals to airports that do not have pipelines. Airports without fuel hydrant systems use trucks to move fuel to aircraft. Due to volumes and cost, it is preferred to use trucks to move fuels short distances. Jet fuel is moved within the United States primarily by pipelines. Movement data is reported between U.S. Petroleum Administration for Defense Districts (PADD). PADDs were originally established during World War II to ration gasoline and evolved to serve as aggregated geographic divisions for transportation data reporting. Figure 17 shows the large movements from PADD 3 to PADDs 1 and 2 (EIA 2025l). Figure 17 also highlights that the United States is a net exporter of jet fuel. The reasons for high imports to PADD 5 are high demand and insufficient pipeline capacity to move fuel from PADD 3 (EIA 2025m). Exports from PADD 5 are primarily to Canada and Mexico (2025n). Publicly available rail, barge, and tanker rates are limited, and pipeline rates must be obtained from each company. There is not a direct correlation between rates and distances as both volume and competition impact rates. The Federal Energy Regulatory Commission requires pipeline companies to publish their rates. Rail rates can be requested by government agencies from the Surface Transportation Board Office of Economics (Surface Transportation Board 2025); barge and tanker rates are known to fluctuate and are not published.
